transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-15
Start: 10:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Nair, Miguel Torres (Redwood) — Samantha Lee, Rob Patel, Dana Moore, Evan Cho (BrightCart)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Reviewed latest KV/prefix cache runs; observed hit-rate improvements after prompt normalization.
- Discussed caching key strategy (prefix normalization, user/context IDs), TTLs, eviction and shard locality.
- SE will run longer benchmark; AE to update pricing and Dedicated recommendation.
- Customer to share prompt templates; plan deep-dive on eviction and SOC2 notes next week.

Topics: prefix cache hit rate, KV cache hit rate, prompt reuse strategy, eviction, TTLs, dedicated vs hosted economics, next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. this is the weekly caching sync for the BrightCart poc. I think we have about 45 minutes on the calendar so we'll kick off, quick round of intros if any new faces?
[00:12] Samantha Lee: Hi yeah Samantha here, Head of ML. Evan is our SRE, Rob is platform, Dana product — thanks.
[00:20] Alex Chen: great. Priya from our infra team will walk through the numbers we ran this week. Priya?
[00:26] Priya Nair: yeah hi, um so quick TL;DR, after applying prefix normalization and a small prompt templating change we saw prefix cache hit-rate jump to ~72% from about 54% baseline, KV cache hit-rate sits at ~61% up from ~48%. those are aggregated across user sessions across the test set.
[00:46] Rob Patel: can you run those numbers again slower, what exactly are you calling prefix vs KV here?
[00:51] Priya Nair: sure, sorry. prefix cache is our prefix/KV hybrid: we store the tokenized prefix sequences keyed by normalized prompt template + user persona, so when a prompt reuses the same template we can reuse the KV cache. KV cache hit rate is measured at the runtime layer where we look up cached KV for the running model instance, prefix hit-rate is higher-level grouping.
[01:12] Samantha Lee: the 72% is across the pilot data? like including rare queries?
[01:16] Priya Nair: yes, it's across the 50k sample set we used. if you look at heavy tail distribution, top 200 templates account for ~63% of traffic, which is why we asked for your top templates export.
[01:28] Dana Moore: right, we can extract the templates and frequency counts. Rob will take point.
[01:33] Rob Patel: yep I'll get that to you. question — how sensitive is the cache to small prompt variations, like punctuation or slot order?
[01:39] Priya Nair: that's exactly why normalization matters. we do whitespace collapse, lowercase, and slot mapping so currency tokens and dates map to placeholders. small changes like an extra hyphen still can bust the key if not normalized, so there's a tradeoff between aggressive normalization and losing signal.
[01:52] Alex Chen: and we saw some cases where over-normalization reduced quality on a handful of templates, so the suggestion is tiered normalization: aggressive for high-volume templates, conservative for low-volume or ML-sensitive prompts.
[02:04] Evan Cho: on SRE side we're interested in eviction and TTL, what's your recommended TTLs for session-based flows?
[02:10] Priya Nair: for session flows we recommend short TTLs — 10 to 30 minutes — because the KV cache can be big and sessions are usually short. for global/shared templates we set longer TTLs like 24 hours. But these are tuning knobs; we're happy to test with your traffic shape.
[02:25] Samantha Lee: do you have the latency numbers correlated with hit-rate? like p95 or p50 improvements?
[02:30] Priya Nair: yes. with the 72% prefix hit and 61% KV hit we saw median token latency drop from ~80ms to ~54ms, and p95 for generation steps dropped from ~420ms to ~310ms in our sim environment. end-to-end request latency improvement averaged ~18-22% depending on sequence length.
[02:50] Rob Patel: ok good. what about the overhead of key lookups, is it negligible?
[02:54] Priya Nair: the additional memcache lookup adds ~2-5ms per request when miss, but on hits you avoid the full KV recompute which is heavy. net improvement is positive as long as hit-rate > ~30-35% for our model configs.
[03:09] Alex Chen: another nuance — batching interacts with cache reuse. when you batch dissimilar prompts you lose opportunities to reuse KV within the batch. Priya, we had some notes about adaptive batching?
[03:20] Priya Nair: right, we propose workload-aware batching where we group by cache key affinity where possible; that increases GPU utilization and preserves cache reuse. we also recommend a small per-worker LRU to keep hot keys local to the worker.
[03:33] Samantha Lee: how hard is that to implement in our Dedicated sim?
[03:36] Priya Nair: on Redwood Dedicated it's straightforward — our routing layer already supports affinity buckets, we just need to expose config. for Hosted there are constraints but we can do probabilistic routing.
[03:45] Dana Moore: you mentioned shard locality — what about multi-region users? we need to keep data residency concerns in mind.
[03:50] Alex Chen: yeah for BrightCart EU customers we can pin to region; for private deployments we support VPC and customer KMS (CMEK). Miguel can follow up on the SOC2/KMS notes after.
[03:59] Miguel Torres: I'll capture that, we did get a few security questions last week. we will surface the SOC2 and KMS notes in the shared doc.
[04:05] Rob Patel: back to cache keys — do you include user IDs in keys? that could explode cardinality.
[04:10] Priya Nair: we generally prefer persona-level keys or session-level keys rather than raw user IDs. including user id is optional and should be used only when per-user personalization is required. otherwise use template+context hash.
[04:22] Samantha Lee: what's your recommendation for eviction policy? LRU vs TTL-based?
[04:26] Priya Nair: TTL is easier operationally, LRU helps when you have bursty traffic. a hybrid approach works well: TTL for coarse control and LRU for hot set management. also we can pin a small set of very hot templates to avoid eviction.
[04:39] Evan Cho: any logs or tracing to measure cache effectiveness in production?
[04:42] Priya Nair: yes we emit token-level hit/miss metrics, per-route hit rates, and per-model KV efficiencies. we can add additional tracing hooks into the console dashboard — you'll get per-template charts once you upload the template list.
[04:55] Dana Moore: about costs — how does caching change cost math for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[04:59] Alex Chen: good question. caching reduces tokens processed by the model which is the main driver of cost. For Hosted usage-based billing you see immediate per-token savings. For Dedicated it's about throughput: higher effective throughput reduces required GPU pool size and thus monthly commit. Priya will include cost-assumption numbers in the benchmarking doc.
[05:16] Priya Nair: I already put a few scenarios in the benchmarking sheet: assumptions include cold miss cost, average sequence length, and hit-rate. link is in the shared folder: https://redwood.app/s/BC-poc-benchmarks (note: placeholder link in transcript).
[05:28] Rob Patel: perfect, we'll look. can you run the longer 24h benchmark you mentioned? to catch diurnal patterns?
[05:33] Priya Nair: yes that's in the next step — running a 24h run with 30k unique prefixes to account for tail effects. expected finish by Friday.
[05:42] Samantha Lee: also we want to test prompt reuse with a live user session flow; can you simulate session continuity?
[05:47] Priya Nair: yes we can replay session traces to validate session TTLs and warm-up behavior. please share your session logs or a sanitized sample.
[05:55] Alex Chen: quick note on prompt templating strategy — customer should aim to reduce unique prompt variants by using slot placeholders where possible; we can provide a small script to normalize.
[06:05] Dana Moore: that's doable but product needs to validate UX. we'll share top templates first.
[06:10] Rob Patel: on the SOC2/KMS front — Miguel can you clarify what you need from our security team?
[06:14] Miguel Torres: primarily we need confirmation on KMS integration (CMEK), and audit log requirements. we'll send a short questionnaire and SOC2 summary.
[06:22] Samantha Lee: timeline — if all goes well with the benchmarks and templates, what's a realistic pilot end and start of production?
[06:28] Alex Chen: for a mid-size customer like BrightCart, a 6-8 week pilot with performance tuning usually leads to a small Dedicated commit if the economics align. we can compress if you want a faster path.
[06:38] Dana Moore: ok. one last technical — when you say KV cache we saw variability across model variants (13B vs 30B), do you recommend any quantization?
[06:45] Priya Nair: quantization reduces GPU memory so it affects latency and batch sizes. for caching the main difference is KV size per token; lower precision reduces KV memory which helps hit-rate per GPU. we can recommend quant profiles per model in the report.
[06:58] Rob Patel: awesome. any blockers from Redwood side?
[07:01] Priya Nair: not from infra; we need the template list and permission to run the longer benchmark on your sample traffic.
[07:08] Alex Chen: ok let's recap and capture action items.
[07:12] Recap (Alex Chen): 1) SE to run 24h KV/prefix benchmark (Priya) 2) BrightCart to share top 200+ templates & frequency (Rob) 3) AE to share updated pricing & Dedicated recommendation (Alex) 4) Security follow-up on SOC2/KMS (Miguel) 5) Schedule eviction deep-dive (calendar invite)
[07:36] Samantha Lee: that sounds good. please add estimated savings in dollars for each scenario in the sheet so we can present to finance.
[07:42] Alex Chen: will do. Priya will include cost assumptions.
[07:45] Dana Moore: thanks everyone. we'll aim to have the template list by Monday.
[07:49] Alex Chen: thanks team, we'll share notes and I'll follow up on pricing. bye.
[07:53] [meeting ends]
